# What Is a Theory? {#what-is-theory}

A regional grocery chain notices that its best-performing stores employ more
staff per square metre than its worst-performing stores. The operations team
proposes adding staff everywhere. The finance team objects: perhaps busy stores
were *given* more staff because they were already busy. A third executive
suggests that the real driver is the store manager — good managers both hire well
and sell more. A fourth points out that the comparison mixes urban and rural
stores, which differ in almost everything. Four people, one correlation, four
different accounts of *what causes what and why*. Each account is a theory, and
the decision the chain makes will depend on which theory it acts on.

This chapter is about what such accounts are, what distinguishes a good one from
a bad one, and how scholars and practitioners can tell the difference. We begin
with what theory is — and, just as importantly, what it is not. We then take
theories apart into their **building blocks** (constructs, relationships,
mechanisms, and boundary conditions), distinguish **types** of theory, set out the
**criteria** by which theories are judged, examine the **levels of analysis** at
which theories operate, and close with how theories change over time. Along the
way we argue a simple thesis: managers do not choose between "theory" and
"practice"; they choose between theories that are explicit, tested, and bounded
and theories that are implicit, untested, and unbounded.

```{r tab-wit-glance}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Concept, ~`Core question`, ~`Key sources`,
  "What theory is (and is not)", "What separates a theory from data, lists, diagrams, or hypotheses?", "Sutton & Staw (1995); Weick (1995); DiMaggio (1995)",
  "Building blocks", "What, how, why, and who/where/when?", "Whetten (1989); Bacharach (1989); Dubin (1978)",
  "Mechanisms", "Through what process does a cause produce its effect?", "Hedstrom & Swedberg (1998); Coleman (1990)",
  "Types of theory", "Does the theory analyse, explain, predict, or prescribe?", "Merton (1968); Gregor (2006)",
  "Criteria for good theory", "Is it falsifiable, useful, parsimonious, general, and interesting?", "Popper (1959); Davis (1971); Corley & Gioia (2011)",
  "Levels of analysis", "At what level do constructs live, and can findings cross levels?", "Rousseau (1985); Klein, Dansereau & Hall (1994)",
  "Theory change", "How do theories and paradigms rise and fall?", "Kuhn (1962); Lakatos (1970)"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Chapter at a glance: the anatomy and evaluation of theory.")
```

## Why Theory Matters {#why-theory-matters}

The word *theory* suffers in everyday speech. "That's just a theory" suggests
speculation; "in theory, yes, but in practice …" suggests irrelevance. In the
sciences the word means something closer to the opposite: a theory is the most
disciplined form of understanding available, an account that has been stated
precisely enough to be checked and has survived attempts to show it wrong.

::: {.definition}
**Theory.** A coherent set of statements about the relationships among constructs,
together with an explanation of *why* those relationships hold and a specification
of the conditions under which they are expected to hold. In Bacharach's
formulation, a theory is a system of constructs and variables in which constructs
are related by propositions and variables by hypotheses, the whole bounded by the
theorist's assumptions [@bacharach1989]. In everyday managerial language,
@christensen2003 offer a compact equivalent: a theory is a statement of what
causes what, and why.
:::

### Managers run on implicit theories

Every managerial decision embeds a causal claim. A sales incentive presumes that
pay shapes effort; a rebrand presumes that perceptions drive choice; a
reorganization presumes that structure shapes coordination. @mcgregor1960 made the
point vividly half a century ago: managers who assume that people dislike work and
must be controlled ("Theory X") design very different organizations from managers
who assume that people seek responsibility under the right conditions ("Theory
Y"). Neither manager thinks of himself or herself as a theorist, yet each acts on a
theory of human motivation — and each theory tends to produce the behaviour it
predicts.

@christensen2003 argue that executives should care about management theory
precisely because they cannot avoid using it. Their critique targets the
"best-practice" habit: copying what successful firms do without understanding the
circumstances in which those practices work. Early attempts at human flight, they
observe, imitated the *attributes* of birds — feathers and flapping wings — rather
than the underlying mechanism of lift. Management advice built on attributes
("successful companies have flat structures") fails in the same way when it is
transplanted to circumstances where the mechanism does not operate. Good theory,
in their account, progresses from describing phenomena, to sorting them into
categories defined by *circumstances* rather than surface attributes, to stating
causal relationships that hold within each category — and it improves fastest
when someone finds an anomaly the existing theory cannot explain.

### Evidence-based management

The **evidence-based management** movement makes the same argument from a
different direction. @rousseau2006 defines it as translating principles based on
the best available evidence into organizational practice, and contrasts it with
decisions grounded in personal preference, imitation, and unsystematic
experience. @pfeffer2006 document how often popular management practices —
forced ranking, merger strategies, pay schemes — are adopted on the strength of
anecdote or fashion rather than evidence. Evidence-based management is not
anti-theoretical; it depends on theory to tell managers which evidence is
relevant to their circumstances and why a finding from one setting should (or
should not) generalize to another.

::: {.business-case}
**Open-plan offices and the theory of collaboration.** Many firms moved to
open-plan offices on the strength of an implicit theory: removing walls increases
chance encounters, encounters increase face-to-face interaction, and interaction
improves collaboration. @bernstein2018 tested the second link directly. Using
wearable sensors and electronic communication records in two corporate
headquarters that switched to open-plan layouts, they found that face-to-face
interaction *fell* sharply after the change while email and messaging rose. A
plausible mechanism is that employees seek privacy when visual exposure
increases. The case illustrates a general lesson: an intuitively appealing causal
chain is a theory, and like any theory it can be wrong in one link even when the
other links are plausible.
:::

## What Theory Is Not {#what-theory-is-not}

A useful way to understand theory is through its imitations. In a widely cited
editorial essay, @sutton1995 identified five things that are often presented as
theory in management manuscripts but are not, on their own, theory. Each is a
legitimate *part* of a theoretical argument; none can substitute for it.

```{r tab-wit-not}
tibble::tribble(
  ~`Not theory on its own`, ~`Why it falls short`, ~`What turns it into theory`,
  "References", "Citing prior work signals which literature a paper belongs to but does not explain anything", "State the logic the cited work supplies and how it applies here",
  "Data", "Data describe which patterns were observed, not why they arose", "Explain the process that generated the pattern",
  "Lists of variables or constructs", "Naming predictors says what matters, not how or why", "Specify relationships and the mechanism linking them",
  "Diagrams", "Boxes and arrows show structure but rarely the reasoning behind each arrow", "Accompany each arrow with an explicit causal argument",
  "Hypotheses or predictions", "Hypotheses state what is expected, not why", "Derive hypotheses from the underlying logic and its assumptions"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Five things that are not theory on their own, following Sutton and Staw (1995).")
```

The common thread is the missing *why*. A paper can be well referenced, rich in
data, and full of diagrams and hypotheses, yet still fail to tell the reader the
causal process that connects one construct to another, or why that process should
operate in some settings but not others. Strong theory, in Sutton and Staw's
account, delves into underlying processes, explores the connections among
phenomena, and tells a story about why acts, events, structures, and thoughts occur.

::: {.debate}
**Theory as product or as process?** Sutton and Staw's essay prompted two
influential replies in the same issue of *Administrative Science Quarterly*.
@weick1995 argued that theory is better seen as a continuum than as a binary:
references, data, lists, diagrams, and hypotheses are often the visible traces of
**theorizing**, an ongoing process whose products are approximations. Judging only
finished theory, he warned, may discourage the interim work from which theory
grows. @dimaggio1995 distinguished three conceptions of theory — theory as
*covering laws* (general statements that subsume particulars), theory as
*enlightenment* (a way of seeing that reveals what was hidden), and theory as
*narrative* (an account of how a process unfolds) — and argued that the most
valuable theories combine elements of all three. The exchange remains a useful
reminder that standards for theory depend partly on the stage of a research
programme. Weick's earlier essay describes theory construction itself as
"disciplined imagination": generating many conjectures and selecting among them
with explicit criteria [@weick1989].
:::

## The Building Blocks of Theory {#theory-building-blocks}

If theory is not a list, a diagram, or a hypothesis, what is it made of? The most
widely used answer in management comes from @whetten1989, who proposed that a
complete theory answers four questions. Earlier, @dubin1978 had laid out a
similar architecture of units, laws of interaction, boundaries, and system
states; and @bacharach1989 sharpened the distinction between the abstract and the
observable parts of a theory.

### What, how, why, and who/where/when

```{r tab-wit-whetten}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Element, ~Question, ~`What it supplies`, ~`Illustration: resource-based theory`,
  "What", "Which factors (constructs) logically belong in the explanation?", "Comprehensiveness balanced against parsimony", "Firm resources and capabilities; competitive advantage",
  "How", "How are the factors related?", "Direction, form, and often causality of relationships", "Resources that are valuable, rare, and costly to imitate lead to sustained advantage",
  "Why", "What psychological, economic, or social dynamics justify the relationships?", "The mechanism; the theory's explanatory core", "Imperfect imitability (causal ambiguity, path dependence, social complexity) blocks competitive erosion",
  "Who / where / when", "To which actors, settings, and times does the theory apply?", "Boundary conditions; limits of generalizability", "Markets with resource heterogeneity and imperfect factor mobility; advantage can erode when environments shift"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Whetten's (1989) four elements of a complete theory, illustrated with resource-based theory (Wernerfelt, 1984; Barney, 1991).")
```

Whetten placed particular weight on the *why*. The *what* and *how* together
describe a theory's domain — they could be read off a diagram — but the *why*
supplies the reasons a reader should believe the diagram, and it is the element
reviewers most often find missing. Resource-based theory illustrates the four
elements well: @Wernerfelt_1984 and @barney1991 identify the constructs (resources
and competitive advantage), the relationship (certain resources produce
sustained advantage), the mechanism (imitation is blocked), and the conditions
(resource heterogeneity and immobility). Later work refined each element
[@Barney_2001; @Barney_2011; @Kozlenkova_2013], a pattern typical of productive
theories.

### Constructs and variables

::: {.definition}
**Construct.** An abstract concept, deliberately invented or adopted for a
scientific purpose, that cannot be observed directly (e.g., *trust*, *brand
equity*, *absorptive capacity*). **Variable.** An observable, measurable
operationalization of a construct (e.g., a five-item trust scale, a price premium,
R&D intensity). **Measure.** The concrete instrument or data source that produces
values of the variable.
:::

Bacharach's distinction between the two levels of a theory is essential for
reading and writing research [@bacharach1989]. **Constructs** are related to one
another by **propositions**; **variables** are related to one another by
**hypotheses**. A proposition ("customer trust increases loyalty") is a claim
about the world at the level of concepts; a hypothesis ("respondents' scores on
the trust scale predict repurchase within twelve months") is a claim about
measured data. Because the link from construct to variable is never perfect, every
empirical test is simultaneously a test of the theory *and* of the measurement
assumptions — a point that returns in Chapter \@ref(using-theory) under the
heading of construct validity.

@suddaby2010 argues that many theories in management suffer from poor **construct
clarity**: constructs are defined loosely, overlap with neighbouring constructs,
or shift meaning across studies. Clear constructs have precise definitions, a
stated scope (the conditions under which the construct applies), explicit
relationships to other constructs, and coherence with the theory's broader logic.
Table \@ref(tab:tab-wit-ladder) illustrates the ladder from construct to measure
across business functions.

```{r tab-wit-ladder}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Function, ~Construct, ~Variable, ~`Example measure`,
  "Marketing", "Brand equity", "Price premium over a private-label equivalent", "Scanner-panel prices for matched products",
  "Strategy", "Absorptive capacity", "R&D intensity; prior related knowledge", "R&D spend divided by sales",
  "HR / OB", "Psychological safety", "Team members' perception that interpersonal risk is safe", "Multi-item survey scale aggregated to the team",
  "Finance", "Information asymmetry", "Dispersion of analysts' earnings forecasts", "Standard deviation of forecasts for a firm-year",
  "Operations", "Process flexibility", "Number of products a plant can switch among", "Plant-level product-assignment records",
  "Information systems", "Perceived usefulness", "User beliefs that a system improves performance", "Validated survey items"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "From construct to variable to measure: the two levels of a theory (following Bacharach, 1989).")
```

### Propositions, hypotheses, and assumptions

Propositions and hypotheses differ in abstraction, not in importance. A theory
paper may advance only propositions; an empirical paper translates them into
hypotheses that a particular dataset can test. Both rest on **assumptions** —
statements the theorist takes as given rather than tests. @bacharach1989
emphasizes that the theorist's implicit values and the spatial and temporal
bounds of a theory are among its most consequential assumptions. Agency theory,
for instance, assumes self-interested agents and goal conflict; stewardship
theory relaxes the first assumption and therefore predicts different governance
arrangements (see [Agency theory](#agency-theory) and
[Stewardship theory](#stewardship-theory)).

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-wit-anatomy) assembles these building blocks into one
picture, using a signaling example developed fully in Chapter \@ref(information).
The upper row is the theory proper; the lower row is its empirical shadow.

```{r fig-wit-anatomy, fig.cap = "The anatomy of a theory. Constructs (upper row) are linked by propositions and a mechanism; boundary conditions moderate the mechanism; each construct is operationalized by a measured variable (lower row), and variables are linked by testable hypotheses. Example drawn from signaling theory (Spence, 1973; Connelly et al., 2011)."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  X  [label = "Construct A\\nWarranty generosity", %s]
  M  [label = "Mechanism (why)\\nCostly commitment that\\nlow-quality sellers avoid", %s]
  Y  [label = "Construct B\\nPerceived product quality", %s]
  B  [label = "Boundary condition\\nInformation asymmetry\\n(new vs. established brand)", %s]
  VX [label = "Variable\\nWarranty length (years)", fillcolor = "#ffffff", color = "#8a8984", style = "rounded,filled,dashed"]
  VY [label = "Variable\\nQuality rating (1-7 scale)", fillcolor = "#ffffff", color = "#8a8984", style = "rounded,filled,dashed"]
  {rank = same; X; VX}
  {rank = same; Y; VY}
  X -> M [label = " proposition"]
  M -> Y
  B -> M [style = dashed, label = " moderates"]
  X -> VX [style = dotted, arrowhead = none, label = " operationalized as"]
  Y -> VY [style = dotted, arrowhead = none]
  VX -> VY [label = " hypothesis (tested)", color = "#8a8984"]
', node_construct, node_mechanism, node_outcome, node_moderator))
```

### Mechanisms: opening the black box

A theory that says *X leads to Y* without saying how is a **black-box** theory. A
**mechanism** is the set of entities and activities, organized in a particular
way, that brings about the effect [@hedstrom1998]. Mechanism-based explanation
became a programme in analytical sociology because correlations between macro
variables — religion and economic development, inequality and crime, firm size
and innovation — say little about the processes that generate them. Specifying
the mechanism makes a theory more credible (because the process is plausible),
more testable (because intermediate steps can be measured), and more useful
(because managers can intervene on the process itself).

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Macro-level associations should be explained by showing how macro
conditions shape individual situations, how individuals act in those situations,
and how individual actions aggregate into macro outcomes.

**Origins.** Sociology; @coleman1990, reconstructing Max Weber's argument linking
Protestant religious doctrine to the rise of capitalism; elaborated as a typology
of social mechanisms by @hedstrom1998.

**Level of analysis.** Explicitly multi-level: macro (society, market,
organization) and micro (individual).

**Key constructs.** Situational mechanism (macro to micro); action-formation
mechanism (micro to micro); transformational mechanism (micro to macro).

**Boundary conditions.** Most useful when the outcome of interest is a collective
property produced by many individual actions; less informative for purely
individual-level phenomena.

**Related theories.** [Social exchange theory](#social-exchange-theory),
[Institutional theory](#institutional-theory),
[Wisdom of the crowd](#wisdom-of-the-crowd).
:::

Coleman's diagram — often called **Coleman's boat** or the "bathtub" — is
redrawn in Figure \@ref(fig:fig-wit-boat). The dashed line across the top is the
observed macro association. Coleman argued that this line is not itself an
explanation; the explanation runs down, across, and back up. Hedström and Swedberg
label the three arrows the **situational**, **action-formation**, and
**transformational** mechanisms [@hedstrom1998].

```{r fig-wit-boat, fig.cap = "Coleman's boat: a macro association (dashed) is explained by a situational mechanism (macro to micro), an action-formation mechanism (micro to micro), and a transformational mechanism (micro to macro). Labels follow Weber's Protestant-ethic example as reconstructed by Coleman (1990) and the typology of Hedstrom and Swedberg (1998).", fig.height = 4.6}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  MA [label = "Macro condition\\n(e.g., Protestant religious\\ndoctrine)", %s]
  MB [label = "Macro outcome\\n(e.g., capitalist economic\\norganization)", %s]
  IA [label = "Individual situation\\n(values, beliefs,\\nopportunities)", %s]
  IB [label = "Individual action\\n(e.g., disciplined work,\\nsaving, reinvestment)", %s]
  {rank = same; MA; MB}
  {rank = same; IA; IB}
  MA -> MB [style = dashed, label = " observed macro association", constraint = false]
  MA -> IA [label = " 1. situational\\n mechanism"]
  IA -> IB [label = " 2. action-formation\\n mechanism"]
  MB -> IB [dir = back, label = " 3. transformational\\n mechanism"]
', node_construct, node_outcome, node_mechanism, node_mechanism), rankdir = "TB")
```

::: {.business-case}
**Illustrative scenario: forced ranking and collaboration.** A firm adopts a
forced-distribution appraisal system (a macro, organization-level policy). The
macro association the board observes a year later is lower cross-unit
collaboration. Coleman's boat structures the explanation. *Situational
mechanism:* the policy turns colleagues into competitors for a fixed number of
top ratings, changing how each employee perceives the payoff to helping others.
*Action-formation mechanism:* employees who believe that helping a peer may cost
them a rating rationally help less and share knowledge more selectively.
*Transformational mechanism:* many such individual choices aggregate into thin
cross-unit networks and slower knowledge flows. Each arrow suggests a different
intervention — redesign the policy, change the individual payoff (e.g., reward
helping explicitly), or build structures that make collaboration less dependent on
discretionary effort.
:::

### Boundary conditions

No theory holds everywhere. **Boundary conditions** specify the actors, settings,
and times for which a theory's relationships are expected to hold — Whetten's
*who, where,* and *when* [@whetten1989]. In empirical work, boundary conditions are
often represented as **moderators**: variables that change the strength or
direction of a relationship. Stating boundary conditions is not an admission of
weakness. A theory that claims to hold everywhere is either trivially true or
unfalsifiable; a theory that states where it stops is both more credible and more
useful, because it tells a manager when *not* to rely on it.

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-wit-boundary) shows the logic for the signaling example.
Warranty generosity should matter a great deal when buyers know little about a
seller (a new entrant) and much less when buyers already have abundant
information (an established brand), because the warranty's signal value depends
on the information gap it closes.

```{r fig-wit-boundary, fig.cap = "Illustrative boundary condition. The effect of warranty length on perceived quality is steep when information asymmetry is high (new entrant) and nearly flat when it is low (established brand). Stylised simulated data; lines are least-squares fits.", fig.height = 4}
set.seed(1989)
n <- 80
bnd <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(warranty = runif(n, 0, 5), group = "New entrant (high asymmetry)") |>
    mutate(quality = 35 + 7.5 * warranty + rnorm(n, 0, 5)),
  data.frame(warranty = runif(n, 0, 5), group = "Established brand (low asymmetry)") |>
    mutate(quality = 58 + 1.2 * warranty + rnorm(n, 0, 5))
)
lab <- bnd |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(fit = predict(lm(quality ~ warranty), newdata = data.frame(warranty = 5)))
ggplot(bnd, aes(warranty, quality, colour = group)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45, size = 1.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_text(data = lab, aes(x = 5.05, y = fit, label = group), hjust = 0, size = 3.3,
            colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("New entrant (high asymmetry)" = pal[["blue"]],
                                 "Established brand (low asymmetry)" = pal[["orange"]])) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 8.2), breaks = 0:5) +
  labs(x = "Warranty length (years)", y = "Perceived quality (index)",
       title = "A boundary condition changes the slope, not just the level",
       subtitle = "Signal value depends on how much the buyer already knows",
       caption = "Stylised data (set.seed(1989)); not empirical estimates.") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

### Variance and process theories

Most of the theories discussed so far take the form of **variance theories**:
they explain variation in an outcome by variation in its antecedents ("the more
X, the more Y, under condition Z"). @mohr1982 contrasted variance theories with
**process theories**, which explain an outcome as the result of a sequence of
events unfolding over time, where the order and timing of events matter and the
necessary conditions need not be sufficient. A variance theory of mergers might
relate acquirer experience to post-merger performance; a process theory would
describe how integration teams, early decisions about systems and leadership, and
emerging conflicts sequence into success or failure.

The two forms answer different questions and call for different evidence.
Variance theories are naturally tested with cross-sectional or panel regressions
and experiments; process theories are built and tested with longitudinal case
studies, event-sequence data, and narrative analysis. @langley1999 reviews
strategies for theorizing from process data, from narrative and visual mapping to
temporal bracketing and quantification of events. For managers, the distinction is
practical: a variance theory says *which* levers matter; a process theory says
*when* and *in what order* to pull them. Many business failures — a sound
strategy launched before the organization could absorb it, a pricing change
introduced before customers understood the value proposition — are failures of
sequencing that a variance theory cannot see.

::: {.pitfall}
**Boxes and arrows without a why.** The most common weakness in theory sections
is a model diagram whose arrows are justified only by citations ("prior research
has found that X affects Y"). A citation shows that a relationship has been
observed; it does not explain it. For every arrow, write one or two sentences
stating the mechanism and one sentence stating when the mechanism should weaken.
If you cannot, the arrow is an empirical conjecture, not theory.
:::

::: {.try-it}
Pick a management idea you have encountered recently — "remote work lowers
innovation", "subscriptions increase customer lifetime value", "diverse boards
improve decisions". Write it out using Whetten's four elements: list the
constructs (*what*), state the relationship (*how*), specify the mechanism
(*why*), and name at least two boundary conditions (*who, where, when*). Then
sketch it as a Coleman boat: which arrows are situational, action-formation, and
transformational?
:::

## Types of Theory {#types-of-theory}

Theories differ not only in content but in ambition and purpose. Two distinctions
are especially useful: *scope* (grand versus middle-range) and *goal* (explanation
versus prediction, among others).

### Grand theory and theories of the middle range

@merton1968 argued that sociology had been caught between two unproductive poles:
the minor working hypotheses of everyday research, which accumulate without
integration, and all-inclusive systematic theories that attempt to explain all
social behaviour and are too abstract to be tested. Between them he advocated
**theories of the middle range**: theories limited to a delimited class of
phenomena, abstract enough to generalize across settings but concrete enough to
yield testable propositions. His own examples included reference group theory and
the theory of role-sets.

Most of the theories in this book are middle-range in Merton's sense. Signaling
theory does not try to explain all of economic life, only how informed parties
reveal hidden quality; [optimal distinctiveness theory](#optimal-distinctiveness-theory)
does not explain all of identity, only the tension between assimilation and
differentiation [@Brewer_1991]. The middle range is where theory is most easily
tested, accumulated, and applied — and where most business research operates.

### Gregor's taxonomy of theory types

Writing for information systems, @gregor2006 proposed a taxonomy that applies
well beyond that field. It distinguishes theories by their *primary goal*.

```{r tab-wit-gregor}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Type, ~`Primary goal`, ~`What it offers`, ~`Business illustration`,
  "I. Analysis", "Describe and classify", "Taxonomies, typologies, frameworks", "Porter's generic strategies; Hofstede's cultural dimensions",
  "II. Explanation", "Explain how and why, without precise prediction", "Causal accounts and mechanisms", "Case-based accounts of why incumbents miss disruptive technologies",
  "III. Prediction", "Forecast outcomes without necessarily explaining them", "Accurate forecasts; black-box models", "Machine-learning churn or demand forecasts",
  "IV. Explanation and prediction", "Explain and predict", "Testable causal propositions", "Signaling theory; prospect theory; goal-setting theory",
  "V. Design and action", "Prescribe how to do something", "Methods, design principles, interventions", "A/B testing protocols; incentive-design principles"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Five types of theory distinguished by their primary goal, following Gregor (2006).")
```

The distinction between types II and III deserves emphasis. A model can predict
well without explaining anything: a demand-forecasting algorithm may exploit
weather, search trends, and calendar effects with no account of why consumers
behave as they do. Conversely, a theory can explain well and predict poorly, as in
evolutionary accounts of industries. @shmueli2010 shows that explanatory and
predictive modelling call for different choices about variables, model
complexity, and evaluation. Business analytics increasingly mixes the two, which
makes it important to be explicit about which one a given analysis is attempting.

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-wit-typology) crosses scope with goal to place some familiar
theories. Placement is a matter of judgement, not measurement; the point is that
"theory" spans a wide range of ambitions.

```{r fig-wit-typology, fig.cap = "A stylised map of theories by scope (grand vs. middle-range; Merton, 1968) and primary goal (explanatory vs. predictive emphasis; Gregor, 2006). Placements are the author's illustrative judgements, not measurements.", fig.height = 5}
quad <- data.frame(
  xmin = c(0, 1, 0, 1), xmax = c(1, 2, 1, 2), ymin = c(1, 1, 0, 0), ymax = c(2, 2, 1, 1),
  title = c("Grand / explanatory", "Grand / predictive", "Middle-range / explanatory", "Middle-range / predictive"),
  fill = c("a", "b", "b", "a")
)
items <- data.frame(
  x = c(0.5, 0.5, 1.5, 1.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 1.5, 1.5, 1.5),
  y = c(1.55, 1.3, 1.55, 1.3, 0.62, 0.42, 0.22, 0.62, 0.42, 0.22),
  label = c("Parsonian structural functionalism", "Coleman's rational-choice social theory",
            "Expected-utility theory", "General equilibrium theory",
            "Signaling theory", "Optimal distinctiveness theory", "Upper echelons theory",
            "Bass diffusion model", "Technology acceptance model", "Goal-gradient hypothesis")
)
ggplot() +
  geom_rect(data = quad, aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax, fill = fill),
            colour = "white", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_text(data = quad, aes(x = (xmin + xmax) / 2, y = ymax - 0.12, label = title),
            fontface = "bold", size = 3.7, colour = ink[["primary"]]) +
  geom_text(data = items, aes(x, y, label = label), size = 3.3, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(a = "#eef4fb", b = "#f6f4ff"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0.5, 1.5), labels = c("Explanatory emphasis", "Predictive emphasis"),
                     expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0.5, 1.5), labels = c("Middle-range", "Grand"), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Theories differ in scope and purpose",
       caption = "Illustrative classification; boundaries between cells are fuzzy.") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.text = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

::: {.business-case}
**Prediction without explanation in customer analytics.** A subscription business
can build a churn model that identifies at-risk customers with impressive
accuracy using hundreds of behavioural features. The model is a type III theory:
it predicts but does not explain. Problems arise when managers treat its
predictors as levers. If "number of support tickets" predicts churn, it does not
follow that suppressing tickets reduces churn — tickets may simply reveal
dissatisfaction that has other causes. An explanatory theory (for example, that
churn results from unmet expectations formed at sign-up) suggests different
interventions and different tests. Mature analytics teams therefore pair
predictive models, which target *whom* to act on, with explanatory theory and
experiments, which determine *what* action works.
:::

## What Makes a Theory Good? {#theory-criteria}

If theories differ in type and scope, by what standards should they be judged?
Philosophers of science and management scholars have converged on a set of
criteria that pull in somewhat different directions.

### Falsifiability

@popper1959 proposed that the line between science and non-science is
**falsifiability**: a scientific theory must prohibit some observable states of
affairs, so that observing them would count against it. A theory compatible with
every possible outcome explains nothing. @bacharach1989 applies the criterion to
organizational theory: constructs must be defined clearly enough, and
relationships stated precisely enough, that empirical refutation is possible.
Vague constructs, tautological propositions ("successful firms have the
capabilities needed for success"), and post hoc boundary conditions all
undermine falsifiability.

### Utility: explanation and prediction

Bacharach's second criterion is **utility**, which he splits into *explanatory
potential* (does the theory explain the relationships it addresses, through
clearly specified constructs and mechanisms?) and *predictive adequacy* (does it
anticipate outcomes beyond the observations from which it was built?)
[@bacharach1989]. A theory that merely redescribes its own data has low utility
even if it is technically falsifiable.

### Parsimony, generality, and accuracy

A good theory explains much with little. **Parsimony** favours theories with fewer
constructs and assumptions, other things equal. **Generality** (or scope) favours
theories that apply across many settings. **Accuracy** favours theories whose
predictions match observations closely. @weick1979 popularized Thorngate's
argument that a theory of social behaviour cannot simultaneously maximize
generality, accuracy, and simplicity: gaining on any two typically costs the third.
The trade-off explains why the theory landscape contains both broad, abstract
frameworks and narrow, precise models, and why neither is simply "better".

### Novelty and interestingness

Theories must also be *worth* attention. In a classic essay, @davis1971 argued
that theories are judged interesting when they deny some assumption their
audience holds — when what seems to be the case turns out not to be — and boring
when they affirm what the audience already believes. Prospect theory was
interesting because it contradicted the assumption that decision-makers evaluate
final wealth states consistently [@kahneman1979]; the finding that open offices
reduce face-to-face interaction is interesting because it contradicts the design
intuition behind them [@bernstein2018]. Interestingness is audience-relative: a
result that surprises economists may be obvious to psychologists.

### Usefulness

@corley2011 review how management scholars define a theoretical contribution and
identify two dimensions: **originality**, ranging from incremental to revelatory,
and **utility**, ranging from scientific usefulness (advancing scholarly
conversation) to practical usefulness (informing what practitioners do). They
argue that the field has overweighted scientific utility and call for more
**prescience** — theorizing that anticipates problems managers and societies will
face, rather than only explaining the past.

::: {.business-case}
**Illustrative scenario: an unfalsifiable strategy claim.** A consultancy
publishes a study concluding that "customer-obsessed" companies outperform their
peers. On inspection, firms were classified as customer-obsessed partly on the
basis of strong growth and high customer ratings — the very outcomes the theory
claims to explain. The claim cannot fail: any high performer will be coded as
customer-obsessed after the fact. A falsifiable version would define the
construct independently of the outcome (for instance, by the share of executive
time spent with customers, or by whether product decisions require customer
evidence), measure it *before* performance is observed, and specify what pattern
— such as customer-obsessed firms underperforming in markets where customer
preferences shift rapidly — would count against it. The scenario illustrates
Bacharach's point that falsifiability depends as much on construct definition as
on the hypothesis itself [@bacharach1989].
:::

::: {.try-it}
Choose a theory from later in this book and evaluate it against Table
\@ref(tab:tab-wit-criteria). On which criterion does it score highest? Which
criterion does it sacrifice, and is that sacrifice consistent with Thorngate's
trade-off between generality, accuracy, and simplicity?
:::

```{r tab-wit-criteria}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Criterion, ~`Diagnostic question`, ~`Typical failure`, ~`Key source`,
  "Falsifiability", "What observation would show the theory wrong?", "Tautology; constructs too vague to measure", "Popper (1959); Bacharach (1989)",
  "Explanatory potential", "Does it say why, through a clear mechanism?", "Black-box correlations", "Bacharach (1989); Hedstrom & Swedberg (1998)",
  "Predictive adequacy", "Does it anticipate outcomes beyond its founding data?", "Post hoc fitting; overfitting", "Bacharach (1989); Shmueli (2010)",
  "Parsimony", "Could fewer constructs explain as much?", "Kitchen-sink models", "Weick (1979)",
  "Generality / scope", "How many settings does it cover?", "Context-bound results presented as general", "Merton (1968); Whetten (1989)",
  "Internal consistency", "Do the assumptions and propositions cohere?", "Mutually inconsistent assumptions", "Bacharach (1989)",
  "Interestingness", "Does it challenge an assumption the audience holds?", "Confirming the obvious", "Davis (1971)",
  "Usefulness", "Does it inform scholars, practitioners, or both?", "Theory that changes no one's action", "Corley & Gioia (2011); Christensen & Raynor (2003)"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Criteria for evaluating a theory.")
```

::: {.debate}
**Can a field be too devoted to theory?** @hambrick2007 argued that management's
insistence that every published paper make a novel theoretical contribution has
costs. It discourages the publication of important facts that lack a ready
theoretical explanation, encourages authors to dress up findings in elaborate but
weakly connected theory, and slows the accumulation of replicated empirical
regularities from which better theory could later be built. Others respond that
without theory, facts do not cumulate and cannot be transported to new contexts.
The debate is a useful reminder that the criteria in Table
\@ref(tab:tab-wit-criteria) are ideals in tension, not a checklist to be maximized
simultaneously — a theme that returns in the discussion of replication in
Chapter \@ref(using-theory).
:::

## Levels of Analysis {#levels-of-analysis}

Every theory is a theory *of something*: individuals, dyads, teams, organizations,
networks, industries, or societies. The **level of analysis** is the unit to which
a theory's constructs and generalizations apply. Business phenomena are almost
always nested — employees within teams, teams within firms, firms within
industries and countries — which makes level mistakes both common and costly.

### Three levels that must align

@klein1994 distinguish the **level of theory** (the unit the theory seeks to
explain), the **level of measurement** (the unit to which data are directly
attached), and the **level of statistical analysis** (the unit treated as the
observation in the analysis). Problems arise when these are misaligned — for
example, when a theory about *team* climate is tested with individual survey
responses analysed as independent observations. Klein and colleagues also show
that a level-specific theory carries an implicit assumption about how members of a
higher-level unit relate to it: members may be **homogeneous** (alike within the
unit, so the unit is the relevant level), **independent** of the unit (so the
individual is the relevant level), or **heterogeneous** within the unit (so
position relative to the group matters, as in a frog-pond model).

### Emergence and cross-level models

@rousseau1985 distinguished **composition models**, which specify how a construct
at one level relates to a functionally similar construct at another (e.g.,
individual perceptions of climate and organizational climate), from
**cross-level models**, which relate constructs at one level to outcomes at
another, and **multilevel models**, which claim that a relationship holds at
several levels. @kozlowski2000 add the concept of **emergence**: higher-level
properties that arise from the interactions of lower-level elements. Emergence
can be *compositional*, when the higher-level construct is essentially the shared
version of the lower-level one (team efficacy as shared individual efficacy), or
*compilational*, when the higher-level construct is a configuration different in
kind from its parts (a team's coordination pattern, which no individual
possesses).

### Cross-level fallacies

Two inferential errors recur. The **ecological fallacy** infers individual-level
relationships from aggregate data. @robinson1950 provided the classic
demonstration: across US states, the proportion of foreign-born residents was
*negatively* correlated with illiteracy, while among individuals foreign birth was
*positively* associated with illiteracy — immigrants tended to settle in states
whose native-born residents were more literate. The opposite error, sometimes
called the **atomistic** or **individualistic fallacy**, infers group-level
relationships from individual data. Figure \@ref(fig:fig-wit-ecological) shows how
the two levels can point in opposite directions.

```{r fig-wit-ecological, fig.cap = "Illustrative cross-level reversal. Across business units, units with higher average workload show higher average service quality (orange), perhaps because high-performing units attract more demand. Within each unit, employees carrying more cases than their colleagues deliver lower quality (blue). Stylised simulated data.", fig.height = 4.2}
set.seed(1950)
units <- data.frame(unit = paste("Unit", 1:5), mu = c(12, 16, 20, 24, 28))
emp <- units[rep(1:5, each = 30), ] |>
  mutate(workload = mu + rnorm(n(), 0, 2.2),
         quality = 40 + 1.4 * mu - 1.6 * (workload - mu) + rnorm(n(), 0, 2.2))
unit_means <- emp |> group_by(unit) |> summarise(workload = mean(workload), quality = mean(quality))
ggplot(emp, aes(workload, quality)) +
  geom_point(colour = ink[["muted"]], alpha = 0.55, size = 1.6) +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = unit, colour = "Within units (individual level)"), method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_smooth(data = unit_means, aes(colour = "Between units (unit level)"), method = "lm", se = FALSE,
              linewidth = 1.1, linetype = "dashed", fullrange = TRUE) +
  geom_point(data = unit_means, colour = pal[["orange"]], size = 3.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Within units (individual level)" = pal[["blue"]],
                                 "Between units (unit level)" = pal[["orange"]]), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Workload (cases per week)", y = "Service quality (index)",
       title = "The same variables, opposite relationships at two levels",
       caption = "Stylised data (5 units x 30 employees; set.seed(1950)); not empirical estimates.")
```

::: {.business-case}
**Engagement surveys and the level of inference.** @harter2002 meta-analysed the
relationship between employee satisfaction and engagement and business outcomes
— customer satisfaction, productivity, profit, turnover, and safety — at the level
of **business units**, finding generalizable positive relationships. The level of
the evidence matters for how managers use it. The findings support unit-level
claims (units with more engaged workforces tend to perform better) and unit-level
interventions (improving local management practices). They do not, by themselves,
establish that any given employee would perform better if made more engaged, nor
do they settle the direction of causality, since well-performing units may also
make work more engaging. Reading the evidence at the right level is the
difference between a sound engagement programme and an overreaching one.
:::

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Checklist for levels in a research design.**

- *State the focal level* of each construct in the theory section, and justify it.
- *Specify the composition model* when aggregating (e.g., direct consensus, referent
  shift, dispersion), and report within-group agreement before aggregating.
- *Align* the levels of theory, measurement, and analysis, or explain and model
  the misalignment.
- *Model nesting* explicitly (multilevel or hierarchical models, clustered standard
  errors, fixed effects for higher-level units).
- *Guard against both fallacies*: do not draw individual conclusions from unit
  data or unit conclusions from individual data without a cross-level argument.
:::

### A map of the book by level

The theories in this book can be organized by the level at which they primarily
operate. Table \@ref(tab:tab-wit-map) serves as a navigational map. Many theories
span levels — signaling theory has been applied to individuals, firms, and
nations — so the "dominant level" column indicates centre of gravity, not
exclusive domain.

## How Theories Change {#how-theories-change}

Theories are not discovered once and then preserved; they are proposed, tested,
amended, combined, and sometimes abandoned. Understanding how this happens helps
readers place any single theory in its intellectual trajectory.

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Science alternates between long periods of **normal science**,
conducted within a shared paradigm, and occasional **revolutions** in which an
accumulation of anomalies leads a community to adopt a new paradigm.

**Origins.** History and philosophy of science; @kuhn1962.

**Level of analysis.** Scientific community and discipline.

**Key constructs.** Paradigm; normal science; puzzle-solving; anomaly; crisis;
revolution; incommensurability.

**Boundary conditions.** Developed from the history of the natural sciences; its
fit to the social sciences, where several paradigms often coexist, is debated.

**Related theories.** Lakatos's methodology of research programmes
[@lakatos1970]; Popper's falsificationism [@popper1959].
:::

@kuhn1962 argued that mature sciences are organized around **paradigms**: shared
exemplars, assumptions, and methods that define which problems are legitimate and
what counts as a solution. Within a paradigm, scientists solve puzzles rather than
test foundations. Anomalies — observations the paradigm cannot accommodate — are
initially set aside or explained away. When they accumulate, a crisis may follow,
and a new paradigm can replace the old one. Kuhn controversially argued that
competing paradigms can be partly **incommensurable**, so that the choice between
them is not settled by data alone. Figure \@ref(fig:fig-wit-kuhn) summarizes the
cycle.

```{r fig-wit-kuhn, fig.cap = "The Kuhnian cycle of theory change (after Kuhn, 1962). Normal science proceeds within a paradigm until anomalies accumulate; a crisis can lead to a revolution and a new period of normal science. Lakatos (1970) offers a gradualist alternative in which research programmes progress or degenerate."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  N [label = "Normal science\\n(puzzle-solving within\\na paradigm)", %s]
  A [label = "Anomalies\\naccumulate", %s]
  C [label = "Crisis\\n(confidence in the\\nparadigm erodes)", %s]
  R [label = "Revolution\\n(new paradigm\\nadopted)", %s]
  N -> A -> C -> R
  R -> N [label = " new normal science", constraint = false, style = dashed]
', node_construct, node_mechanism, node_mechanism, node_outcome))
```

@lakatos1970 proposed a less dramatic account. Scientific **research programmes**
consist of a *hard core* of assumptions protected by a *belt* of auxiliary
hypotheses that absorb anomalies. A programme is *progressive* when its
modifications predict novel facts and *degenerating* when they merely patch
failures after the fact. The Lakatosian lens fits management and economics well,
where theories are rarely overthrown outright but are amended, bounded, and
gradually displaced.

The history of strategy research illustrates the pattern. Industrial-organization
reasoning, popularized for strategy by Porter, located the sources of
profitability primarily in industry structure [@porter1980industry]. Persistent
performance differences among firms *within* the same industry were an anomaly
for that view, and the resource-based view relocated the explanation inside the
firm [@Wernerfelt_1984; @barney1991]. When critics noted that static resource
endowments could not explain how firms adapt to rapid change, the
dynamic-capabilities framework extended the programme [@teece1997]. Each shift
retained much of its predecessor; none was a clean Kuhnian revolution. In
behavioural decision research, by contrast, the accumulation of anomalies for
expected-utility theory produced something closer to a paradigm contest, with
prospect theory offering a descriptive alternative built on reference dependence
and loss aversion [@kahneman1979].

::: {.debate}
**Does management have — or need — a paradigm?** @pfeffer1993 argued that
organizational science suffers from low **paradigm development**: weak consensus
on theories and methods, compared with fields such as economics. In his view, this
fragmentation makes it harder to accumulate knowledge, allocate resources, and
defend the field's standing. Critics countered that theoretical pluralism is
appropriate to a complex subject matter and that enforced consensus could
suppress valuable alternatives. The debate maps onto a practical question for
readers of this book: when theories disagree, should we seek a winner, a synthesis,
or a clear statement of the conditions under which each applies? Chapter
\@ref(using-theory) takes up that question under the heading of competing-theory
tests and strong inference.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Mistaking a fashion for a revolution.** Management ideas often rise and fall
with the business press, and new labels are sometimes presented as paradigm
shifts. Before treating a new framework as a replacement for an established
theory, ask Lakatos's question: does it predict novel facts that the older theory
cannot, or does it re-describe familiar facts in new vocabulary?
:::

## Chapter Summary {#what-is-theory-summary}

::: {.key-takeaways}
- A **theory** is a set of related propositions about constructs, together with an
  explanation of *why* they are related and *where* the relationships hold
  [@whetten1989; @bacharach1989].
- References, data, variable lists, diagrams, and hypotheses are ingredients of
  theory, not substitutes for it; the missing element is usually the *why*
  [@sutton1995], although theorizing is a process whose interim products matter
  [@weick1995].
- **Constructs** are linked by **propositions**; **variables** by **hypotheses**.
  Every empirical test is also a test of measurement.
- **Mechanisms** open the black box; Coleman's boat decomposes macro associations
  into situational, action-formation, and transformational mechanisms
  [@coleman1990; @hedstrom1998].
- Theories vary in **scope** (grand vs. middle-range) and **goal** (analysis,
  explanation, prediction, design) [@merton1968; @gregor2006].
- Good theories are falsifiable, useful, parsimonious, appropriately general, and
  interesting, but these criteria trade off against one another [@popper1959;
  @davis1971; @corley2011].
- Levels of theory, measurement, and analysis must align; relationships can
  reverse across levels [@klein1994; @robinson1950].
- Theories change through revolutions and, more often in management, through the
  progressive or degenerating evolution of research programmes [@kuhn1962;
  @lakatos1970].
- Managers always act on theories; the choice is between explicit, tested theories
  and implicit, untested ones [@christensen2003; @rousseau2006].
:::

```{r tab-wit-summary}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Idea, ~`Core claim`, ~`Practical test`, ~`Key source`,
  "What theory is not", "Ingredients are not explanations", "Can you state the why for each arrow?", "Sutton & Staw (1995)",
  "Four building blocks", "What, how, why, who/where/when", "Are all four explicit?", "Whetten (1989)",
  "Constructs vs. variables", "Propositions link constructs; hypotheses link variables", "Is the construct-to-measure link defensible?", "Bacharach (1989)",
  "Mechanisms", "Explain macro patterns through micro processes", "Can the intermediate steps be observed?", "Coleman (1990); Hedstrom & Swedberg (1998)",
  "Middle-range theory", "Bounded, testable theories accumulate best", "Is the scope stated and testable?", "Merton (1968)",
  "Theory types", "Analysis, explanation, prediction, design", "Is the goal explicit?", "Gregor (2006)",
  "Evaluation criteria", "Falsifiable, useful, parsimonious, interesting", "Which criterion is being traded off?", "Popper (1959); Davis (1971)",
  "Levels of analysis", "Align theory, measurement, analysis", "Is a cross-level inference being made?", "Klein et al. (1994)",
  "Theory change", "Paradigms and research programmes", "Does the new idea predict novel facts?", "Kuhn (1962); Lakatos (1970)"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Summary of the chapter's core ideas.")
```

## Discussion Questions {#what-is-theory-questions}

1. Take a recent empirical article in your field. Using Whetten's four elements,
   identify which element is weakest. What would it take to strengthen it?
2. Sutton and Staw argue that diagrams are not theory, while Weick argues that
   they may be valuable steps in theorizing. Under what circumstances is a
   diagram-heavy paper a genuine contribution?
3. Choose a managerial "best practice" (e.g., open-plan offices, forced ranking,
   loyalty programmes). Reconstruct the implicit theory behind it as a Coleman
   boat. Which arrow is least supported by evidence?
4. A consultancy reports that firms with more diverse boards have higher returns
   on equity. What level-of-analysis and causal questions would you ask before
   recommending board diversification to a specific client?
5. Thorngate's postulate suggests that no theory can be simultaneously general,
   accurate, and simple. Pick one theory from this book and argue which of the
   three it sacrifices.
6. Is the shift from industry-structure explanations to the resource-based view
   better described as a Kuhnian revolution or a Lakatosian progression? Defend
   your answer with evidence.

## Further Reading {#what-is-theory-reading}

- @whetten1989 — a five-page statement of what a theoretical contribution requires;
  the most practical starting point.
- @sutton1995 — a sharp diagnosis of what theory is not, with the replies by
  @weick1995 and @dimaggio1995 in the same issue.
- @bacharach1989 — rigorous criteria for evaluating organizational theories,
  including the construct–variable distinction.
- @hedstrom1998 — the core statement of mechanism-based explanation in the social
  sciences.
- @klein1994 — the standard reference on levels issues in theory, measurement, and
  analysis.
- @davis1971 — why some theories capture attention and others do not; still
  provocative.
- @christensen2003 — a practitioner-oriented argument for why managers need
  explicit causal theory.
- @kuhn1962 — the classic account of paradigms and scientific revolutions.
